title: Humans Watched This Supernova Explode Nearly a Millennium Ago. Now You Can See It in High Definition
gist: Astronomers using the Gemini North telescope produced the sharpest image yet of the Pa 30 nebula, remnant of a supernova recorded in 1181, revealing about ten times more structure and that its filaments are strings of uniform knots. The central 'zombie star' survived the explosion, which could help explain rare supernova physics.

insights.claim: Gemini North observations of the Pa 30 nebula revealed about 10 times more structures than any previous images of the supernova remnant.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Instrument resolution advances are driving new astrophysics; no direct market link.
insights.quote: revealed about 10 times more structures than any previous glimpses
insights.locator: Previous images of the explosion’s remnants

insights.claim: The filaments are not continuous but are beads on a string, made of pearl-like gas knots of relatively uniform size.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Reveals structure that models of supernova ejecta must now explain.
insights.quote: they’re shaped more like beads on a string
insights.locator: Previous images of the explosion’s remnants

insights.claim: Each knot is about four light-days across, large enough to hold the solar system's planetary region about 10 times, according to coauthor Ilaria Caiazzo.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Scale of the structures sets constraints for modelling.
insights.quote: The planetary region of our solar system could fit in each knot about 10 times with room to spare
insights.locator: These “cosmic pearls” are, in fact, enormous.

insights.claim: The knots' regularity in size and alignment along filaments is unexpected since astronomers expected oddly shaped accumulations after a supernova, and could deepen understanding of stellar death.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: An unexplained feature that will drive follow-up modelling.
insights.quote: What’s strange, however, is their regularity.
insights.locator: How exactly the pearls formed is not yet entirely clear

insights.claim: Pa 30's central star survived a thermonuclear supernova that normally destroys a star completely, and scientists do not yet understand why; the structures may help reconstruct such detonations.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Shows rare partial-survival supernovae are a frontier question.
insights.locator: The Pa 30 nebula is also particularly unusual

insights.claim: Pa 30 matches records left by Chinese and Japanese astronomers in 1181 of a new star visible for several months, linking modern observation to medieval accounts.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Historical records anchor the object's age and identification.
